Lottie made up the third member of the little group. Still small, she knew nothing of adversity and was bewildered by the change in her young adopted mother. She had heard whispers of strange events in Sara's life, but could not understand her altered appearance. Why the old black frock? Why did Sara now enter the schoolroom only to teach, instead of sitting in her honoured place to learn? Among the little children there had been a great deal of whispering when they discovered that Sara had left the rooms where Emily had reigned for so long. What most troubled Lottie was how little Sara would say in answer to questions. At seven, you need a mystery explained very plainly indeed before you can understand it.

On the first morning Sara taught the little French class, Lottie had asked in confidence, "Sara, are you terribly poor now? As poor as a beggar?" Slipping her fat hand into Sara's slender one, she gazed up with round eyes full of tears. "I don't want you to be that poor."
She seemed on the point of tears, and Sara quickly tried to comfort her.
"A beggar hasn't anywhere to live," she answered bravely. "I've still got somewhere to live."
Lottie pressed her. "Where is it? The new girl has your bedroom now, and it doesn't look pretty any more."
"My room is somewhere else now," Sara replied.
"Is it pretty?" Lottie asked. "I'd like to come and look at it."
Sara said, "You must be quiet. Miss Minchin is watching. She'll be angry with me if I let you go on whispering."
She had already learned that anything anyone objected to would be counted as her fault. Children talking, fidgeting, or failing to pay attention—all of it would bring a reprimand upon Sara.

But Lottie was a very determined little person. If Sara would not reveal where she lived, she meant to discover it for herself. She questioned her small friends, lingered near the older girls, and listened to their gossip. With some information they had let slip without noticing, she set off late one afternoon on an exploring expedition. Up she climbed, on staircases she had never known were there, until she arrived at the attic floor. Two doors stood close together. Opening one of them, she found her beloved Sara standing on an old table and looking through a window.

"Sara! Mamma Sara!" she cried in horror. The attic appalled her: it was ugly and empty and seemed cut off from the whole world. Her short legs felt as though they had climbed hundreds of steps to reach it.

Hearing the voice, Sara turned, and now she was the horrified one. What was going to happen? If Lottie burst into tears and someone heard her, both of them were lost. Sara sprang off the table and hurried across to her.
"Please don't cry or make any noise," she begged. "They'll scold me if you do, and they've been scolding me all day. It isn't—it isn't really such a bad room, Lottie."

"Isn't it?" Lottie gasped, biting her lip as she surveyed the place. She was still a spoiled little girl, but she loved her adopted mother enough to try to restrain herself for her sake. Besides, perhaps anywhere Sara lived could somehow prove to be nice. Almost in a whisper, she asked, "Why isn't it bad, Sara?"
Sara held her tightly and attempted a laugh. The warmth of that plump little body brought a kind of comfort. Her day had been difficult, and her eyes were hot from staring out through the window.
"Up here you can see all kinds of things that aren't visible downstairs," she told her.
"What kinds?" Lottie demanded, with the curiosity Sara knew how to awaken even in much older girls.

"Chimneys right beside us, with smoke twisting into wreaths and clouds before it drifts into the sky. Sparrows hopping around and chatting together as though they were people. Other attic windows, where a head might appear at any moment, leaving you to wonder whose it is. Everything feels so high above the ground—almost like being in another world."
"Oh, I want to look!" Lottie cried. "Lift me up to see!"
Sara lifted her onto the old table and climbed up beside her. Together they leaned against the edge of the flat roof window and peered outside.

Unless you have looked out like this yourself, you cannot know how different that world is. Roof slates stretched away to either side, sloping down towards the rain gutters. At home among them, the sparrows hopped and twittered without a trace of fear. On the nearest chimney, two perched together and quarrelled furiously until one pecked his companion and chased him off. The neighbouring garret window remained closed: the house beside theirs was empty.

"I wish there were someone living next door," said Sara. "It's so near that if another little girl had that attic, we could speak through our windows. We could even climb across to visit, if we weren't frightened of falling."

The sky looked so much closer than it did from the street that Lottie was entranced. Here at the attic window, surrounded by chimney pots, the world's goings-on below hardly seemed real. It was difficult even to believe in Miss Minchin, Miss Amelia, and the schoolroom. Wheels rumbling through the square sounded as though they belonged to an entirely separate life.
Nestling into Sara's protective arm, Lottie exclaimed, "Oh, Sara! I like being in this attic—I really like it! It's better than being downstairs!"
"See that sparrow," Sara murmured. "I wish I had a few crumbs I could throw out for him."
Lottie gave a tiny shriek. "I've got some! There's a piece of bun in my pocket. I spent my penny on it yesterday and kept a little bit."

They scattered a few crumbs, and the sparrow started and fluttered off to a nearby chimney. Clearly he was unused to friendly neighbours in attics; food arriving without warning had alarmed him. But Lottie held perfectly still, and Sara made a soft chirping sound, almost like a sparrow herself. He began to understand that what had frightened him was really an offer of hospitality. Tilting his head, he watched the crumbs from his chimney perch, his eyes bright and twinkling. Lottie could hardly bear to stay motionless.
"Is he coming? Do you think he'll come?" she whispered.
Sara whispered back, "His eyes seem to say so. He's trying and trying to decide if it's safe. Yes, he's going to! Look, here he comes!"

Down he flew, hopping towards the crumbs, then pausing a few inches short of them. Again he tilted his head, as though calculating the possibility that Sara and Lottie were really large cats ready to spring. At last his heart assured him they were kinder than they appeared. Hop by hop, he came closer. With a peck as quick as lightning, he snatched the largest crumb and flew with it to the far side of his chimney.
"Now he KNOWS it's safe," said Sara. "He'll return to fetch the rest."

Return he did, bringing a friend. That friend went off and fetched a relation, and the whole party enjoyed a substantial meal, twittering, chattering, and exclaiming over it. Now and then they paused, cocked their heads, and inspected Sara and Lottie. Lottie's delight swept away her first horrified impression of the attic. When Sara lifted her down from the table, bringing her back, so to speak, to earthly matters, she could show her all sorts of lovely things about the room that she herself would never have imagined were there.

"It's so small, and so far above everything else," she explained, "that it almost feels like a nest in a tree. And what a funny sloping ceiling. Look—at this end you can barely stand upright. When morning begins, I can stay in bed and see straight into the sky through the flat window overhead. It's a square of light. On a day that's going to be sunny, little pink clouds drift past, so close I feel I might touch them. When it rains, the drops keep pattering as if they were saying something pleasant. At night, when the stars come out, you can lie there counting how many fit inside that square. There are so many. And see that tiny rusty grate in the corner. Imagine it polished, with a fire burning inside—wouldn't that be lovely? You see, it really is a beautiful little room."

Holding Lottie's hand, she moved about the tiny room. Her gestures pointed out the beauties she was persuading herself to see, and Lottie saw them too. Whatever picture Sara drew in words, Lottie could always believe it.

"Imagine a thick, soft Indian rug, blue, covering the floor," she continued. "Over there could be a cosy little sofa with cushions for curling up on. Above it, a bookshelf low enough for you to reach the books without getting up. In front of the fire we could have a fur rug, and on the walls there could be hangings to hide the whitewash, and pictures. The pictures would need to be small, but they could still be beautiful. There could be a lamp under a deep rose-coloured shade, and a table in the centre with everything for tea. A little round copper kettle could sing on the hob. Even the bed could change completely: soft inside, with a lovely silk coverlet over it. How beautiful it might be. Perhaps we could coax the sparrows into becoming such good friends that they'd tap on the window with their beaks and ask us to let them in."
Lottie cried, "Oh, Sara! How I'd love to live up here!"

At last Sara persuaded her to return downstairs and saw her safely on her way. Back in the attic, she stood in the centre and looked around. The spell of the lovely pictures she had made for Lottie had faded. Under its shabby quilt, the bed was hard. The whitewashed walls were broken in patches; the floor lay bare and cold. The grate was damaged and rusty, and the only place to sit was a battered footstool leaning sideways on its broken leg. Sara sank onto it for a few minutes and lowered her head into her hands. Somehow Lottie's visit, and her departure, made everything worse—perhaps as prisoners feel still more lonely after their visitors have come and gone, leaving them behind.
"How lonely it is," she said. "Sometimes nowhere in the world could be lonelier."

As she sat there in that position, a small sound nearby caught her attention. She raised her head to find its source. A more nervous child would have jumped from that battered footstool immediately, for a large rat was sitting back on his hindquarters, sniffing with interest. Some crumbs from Lottie's bun had fallen onto the floor, and their smell had tempted him out of his hole.

His curious appearance fascinated Sara: he looked so like a dwarf or gnome with grey whiskers. His bright eyes met hers as though asking a question. He seemed so uncertain that one of Sara's strange little thoughts came to her.

"Being a rat must be rather difficult," she reflected. "No one likes you. Everyone jumps and runs and screams, 'Oh, a horrid rat!' I wouldn't enjoy people jumping and screaming, 'Oh, a horrid Sara!' as soon as they caught sight of me. Or putting out traps for me and making them look like dinner. How different it is for a sparrow. But when this rat was made, nobody asked whether being a rat was what he wanted. No one said, 'Wouldn't you rather be a sparrow?'"

Sara had remained so still that the rat was beginning to feel braver. He was terribly afraid of her, but perhaps, like the sparrow, he had a heart that could tell him she was not the kind of creature that pounced. And he was very hungry. Inside the wall were his wife and many children; for days they had been having dreadful luck. He had left the little ones crying bitterly. A few crumbs seemed worth a considerable risk, and he carefully lowered himself onto all four feet.
"Come along," Sara told him. "I'm no trap. Have the crumbs, you poor thing! People imprisoned in the Bastille used to befriend rats. Why shouldn't I be friends with you?"

I cannot say how animals understand such things, but understand them they certainly do. Perhaps there is a language without words, known to everything in the world. Perhaps a hidden soul lives in everything and can speak to another soul without the smallest sound. Whatever the explanation, from that instant the rat understood that he was safe, rat though he was. The young human sitting on the red footstool would not leap up and frighten him with piercing cries. She would not hurl heavy things at him, which might crush him where they fell or leave him limping as he scrambled home to his hole. He was, in fact, a very nice rat with no wish to hurt anybody. Standing upright and sniffing, with his bright eyes on Sara, he had hoped she would realize that, instead of hating him at once as an enemy. When the mysterious voice that uses no words assured him that she would understand, he moved gently towards the crumbs and started eating. Now and again he looked up at Sara, just as the sparrows had. There was something so apologetic in his expression that it touched her heart.

She sat watching him without making the slightest movement. Among the crumbs lay one much larger piece—hardly a crumb at all, really. He plainly longed for it, but it was close to the footstool, and some of his shyness remained.
"I think he'd like to take that home to his family in the wall," Sara thought. "Perhaps he'll fetch it if I keep perfectly still."

So intent was she that she barely let herself breathe. The rat edged nearer, ate some smaller crumbs, and paused to sniff delicately, casting a sideways look at the child on the footstool. Then, with a sudden boldness much like the sparrow's, he dashed at the piece of bun. No sooner had he seized it than he ran to the wall, slipped through a crack in the skirting board, and disappeared.
"I was sure it was for his children," Sara said. "I really think we could become friends."

About a week later, Ermengarde found one of her rare safe opportunities to creep up to the attic. She tapped lightly with her fingertips, but Sara took two or three minutes to answer. At first the room was so silent that Ermengarde wondered whether she might be asleep. Then, to her astonishment, she heard a quiet little laugh and Sara's voice coaxing somebody.
"There you are!" she heard Sara say. "Take it home with you, Melchisedec! Off you go to your wife!"
A moment later Sara opened the door. Ermengarde stood on the threshold, staring at her with frightened eyes.
"Sara, who—who ARE you speaking to?" she gasped.
Sara carefully drew her inside, with a look of mingled pleasure and amusement.
"First you must promise you won't be frightened or give even the tiniest scream," she replied. "Otherwise I can't tell you."

Ermengarde almost screamed then and there, but held herself back. She searched the attic with her eyes and could see nobody. Yet Sara had unmistakably been speaking TO somebody. Ghosts came into her mind.
"Is it—is it something frightening?" she asked in a timid voice.
"Some people find them frightening," Sara answered. "I did myself at first, but I don't any more."
Trembling, Ermengarde asked, "Was it—a ghost?"
Sara laughed. "No, it was my rat."
In a single leap Ermengarde landed in the centre of the small, shabby bed. She drew her feet beneath her nightgown and red shawl. No scream came, but she gasped in terror.
Under her breath she cried, "Oh! Oh! A rat! A rat!"
"I thought you might be afraid," said Sara. "But there's no need. I'm teaching him to be tame. He really recognizes me, and when I call, he comes out. Are you too frightened to have a look at him?"

In truth, as the days passed, scraps carried upstairs from the kitchen had helped their unusual friendship grow. Sara had gradually stopped remembering that the shy little creature she was getting to know was, after all, only a rat.

At first Ermengarde could do nothing but curl into a frightened heap on the bed, keeping her feet well tucked away. Gradually, though, Sara's calm little face and her account of Melchisedec's first visit stirred her curiosity. She leaned over the bedside and watched Sara cross the room and kneel beside the hole in the skirting board.
"He—he isn't going to dash out and leap onto the bed, is he?" she asked.
"No," Sara assured her. "His manners are as good as ours. He's exactly like a person. Watch him now!"

A soft whistle came from her lips, so quiet and coaxing that only perfect silence could have made it audible. She repeated it several times, wholly absorbed. To Ermengarde, she seemed to be casting a spell. At length, apparently answering the summons, a grey-whiskered head with bright eyes peered out of the hole. Sara let the crumbs in her hand fall to the floor. Melchisedec emerged without a sound and ate them. One larger piece he picked up and carried home with an air of brisk efficiency.

"That one's for his wife and children, you see," Sara explained. "He's very kind. He keeps only the little crumbs for himself. Whenever he goes home, I hear his family squeaking happily. I can tell three different sorts of squeak: the children's, Mrs. Melchisedec's, and Melchisedec's own."
A laugh escaped Ermengarde.
"Oh, Sara!" she exclaimed. "You really ARE strange—but you're nice."

"I know I'm strange," Sara agreed happily, "and I do TRY to be nice." She passed her small brown paw across her forehead, looking puzzled and tender. "Papa was always laughing at me, and I liked him doing it. He thought I was strange, but he enjoyed my make-believe. I—I can't stop inventing things. Without that, I don't think I could live." She broke off to look around the attic, then added softly, "Certainly not here. I couldn't live here."
As always, Ermengarde listened with interest. "When you describe things," she said, "it's as if they become real. The way you speak of Melchisedec makes him sound like a person."

"But he IS a person," Sara replied. "He feels hunger and fear just like us. He has a wife and children. Who can say he doesn't have thoughts the way we do? His eyes look like a person's eyes to me. That's the reason I named him."
She settled on the floor, clasping her knees in the way she liked best.
"Besides, he's a rat from the Bastille, sent here to befriend me," she added. "There's always a scrap of bread the cook has discarded, and that's quite enough to keep him fed."
Ermengarde asked eagerly, "Is this still the Bastille? Do you pretend you're in the Bastille all the time?"
"Almost all the time," Sara said. "Now and then I try to imagine some different place. Usually the Bastille is easiest, especially in cold weather."
Just then a noise startled Ermengarde so badly that she nearly sprang off the bed. It sounded like two separate knocks against the wall.
"What's making that noise?" she exclaimed.
Rising from the floor, Sara replied with considerable drama:
"The prisoner in the cell beside mine is knocking."
"Becky!" exclaimed Ermengarde in delight.
"Yes," Sara replied. "Listen. Two knocks say, 'Prisoner, are you there?'"
She gave three answering taps against the wall herself.
"And that says, 'Yes, I am here, and all is well.'"
From Becky's side came four taps in reply.
Sara interpreted them: "Those say, 'Then, fellow-sufferer, we will sleep in peace. Good night.'"
Ermengarde's whole face shone with pleasure.
"Oh, Sara!" she whispered happily. "It's just like being in a story!"
"It IS a story," Sara answered. "EVERYTHING'S a story. You're one, and I'm one, and Miss Minchin is a story too."

Sitting down again, she talked on until Ermengarde forgot that she, too, was something of an escaped prisoner. Sara finally had to remind her that she could not spend the entire night in the Bastille: she must slip silently downstairs and steal back into the bed she had left empty.
